items.prompt: Why did the suite go from 4 to 38 minutes?
choices: Each new test added seconds to one serial line
Each old test slowly got slower on its own
The CI machines slowly wore out over the course of the year
items.explanation: Added tests, summed serially: no bad decision needed.

items.prompt: What tends to happen to a suite that is too slow?
choices: Engineers read every result
Engineers rewrite it weekly
Engineers stop running it
items.explanation: A slow suite gets skipped, first locally and then in habit.

items.prompt: What tends to happen to a suite that fails at random?
choices: Failures get fixed at once
Failures get rerun, not read
Failures get ignored by CI itself
items.explanation: Random red teaches people to click rerun and move on.

items.prompt: How many times did the hidden bug fail before anyone looked closer?
items.explanation: It failed 12 times over three weeks, each time rerun to green.

items.prompt: Once rerun-and-hope is the default, a real failure looks like what?
choices: A slow one
A passed one
A false one
items.explanation: When every red gets the same reflex, real and false reds are treated alike.

items.prompt: How long does a serial suite take in total?
choices: The time of its slowest test
The sum of every test's time
The average test time alone
items.explanation: One process, one test at a time: add them all up.

items.prompt: Did the individual tests get worse in this story?
choices: No, the suite as a whole did
Yes, each one got slower
Yes, each one got less correct
items.explanation: The tests were fine. Total time and noise were the problem.

items.prompt: How long did the suite take a year ago?
choices: 11 minutes
38 minutes
4 minutes
items.explanation: It was 4 minutes a year ago and 38 today.

items.prompt: Engineers have stopped running the 38-minute suite locally and just push and wait. Which description fits what has happened to the suite's value?
choices: It stopped being correct, so its assertions need to be rewritten from scratch
It stopped giving fast feedback, so bugs are now found later and at more cost
It stopped being needed, because CI will catch the same bugs without it
It stopped being parallel, so the only remedy is a bigger CI machine
items.explanation: Slowness changes behaviour, not correctness: feedback arrives late, so problems are found later.
items.reference:
Slow and noisy both end the same way
slow suite: gets skipped
noisy suite: gets rerun, not read
result: real failures look like false ones
Why: people stop trusting a signal that costs time or cries wolf, however good each test is.
items.learnMore:
Why a suite loses trust

Runtime grows by addition: every reasonable test adds seconds. The real damage is behavioural. Skipping and rerunning train everyone to treat red as noise.

Common mistake

Blaming individual tests. The tests can all be correct while the suite as a whole stops being believed.
items.reflection: Think of any alarm or warning you have learned to ignore. What first taught you to ignore it, and what would it take to trust it again?

It made the racing background job run less often in CI
It hid a reproducible bug behind a routine that treated it as noise
It deleted the failing test so the bug stopped being reported
items.explanation: The bug was always there. Rerun taught people to look away, so a real failure was filed under noise.

items.prompt: What does sharding do to a suite?
choices: Splits it into slices that run at the same time
Makes every single test in the suite run noticeably faster
Removes the slowest tests from the suite
items.explanation: Shards are disjoint slices run concurrently.

items.prompt: With shards running together, wall-clock time is close to what?
choices: The sum of every shard's time
The average shard's time halved
What the slowest shard takes
items.explanation: The suite finishes when its last shard finishes.

items.prompt: Does sharding make any one test faster?
choices: Yes, because each test gets its very own dedicated CPU
No, it only runs tests side by side
Yes, but only the slowest one
items.explanation: A test still takes as long as it takes.

items.prompt: Which of these counts as per-shard overhead?
choices: Starting up and collecting results
Writing the tests themselves in the first place
Reading the test report later
items.explanation: Each shard pays to start, receive files and report back.

items.prompt: What puts a floor under runtime however many shards exist?
choices: The number of test files
The name of the CI vendor
The single slowest test
items.explanation: One test runs on one shard, so it cannot be split.

items.prompt: What happens to the separate shard results?
choices: They are kept as separate verdicts
They are merged into one CI verdict
They are averaged into a score
items.explanation: The pipeline reports one pass or fail.

items.prompt: Going from 1 to 4 shards on a big suite usually does what?
choices: Pays off a great deal
Barely changes runtime
Makes the suite slower
items.explanation: Large early gains, since each shard does far less work.

items.prompt: In the demo model, about how long does 38 minutes of work take on 4 shards?
choices: About 19 minutes
About 38 minutes
About 10 minutes
items.explanation: 9.5 minutes of work plus 0.4 overhead is about 10.

items.prompt: In the demo model (38 minutes of work, 0.4 minutes overhead per shard, slowest test 1.5 minutes), which change saves the least time?
choices: Going from 1 shard to 2 shards
Going from 32 shards to 40 shards
Going from 4 shards to 8 shards
Going from 8 shards to 16 shards
items.explanation: 32 shards take about 1.59 minutes and 40 take the 1.5 floor, a gain of about 5 seconds. The earlier steps save 19, 4.75 and 2.4 minutes.
items.reference:
Runtime = larger of (work per shard + overhead) and the slowest test
1 shard: 38.4 min
4 shards: 9.9 min
16 shards: 2.78 min
40 shards: 1.5 min, the floor
Why: extra shards shrink the work per shard, but fixed overhead and the slowest test do not shrink.
items.learnMore:
Why sharding flattens out

Wall-clock time follows the slowest shard. Early shards divide a big number, so they help a lot. Later shards divide a small number while each still costs fixed overhead, and one slow test cannot be split.

Common mistake

Expecting runtime to halve every time runners double. That only holds when tests are many, equal-sized and overhead is tiny.
items.reflection: Think of any job you split among helpers, like moving boxes. When did adding a helper stop making it finish sooner, and what was the thing that could not be split?

items.prompt: A suite has one 90-second test. A team keeps adding shards hoping to get below 90 seconds. What happens?
choices: Runtime keeps halving each time shards double, because shards also split a single test in parts
Runtime rises at once, because every extra shard doubles the overhead
Runtime stops near 90 seconds, because that one test runs whole on one shard
Runtime drops to zero, because enough shards make the suite parallel
items.explanation: A single test cannot be spread over shards, so its duration is a hard lower bound.

Run the slow shard twice and take whichever result comes first
Assign tests to shards by recorded duration so the shards finish together

choices: One shard holds the longest tests and finishes well after all the others

Each test file is tiny and every test runs in about the same time
The suite was already running in under a second before the change

items.prompt: What must be true of tests for sharding to be safe?
choices: No test depends on others not running at once
Every test takes exactly the same amount of time to run
Every test uses the same shared fixture
items.explanation: Isolation is the precondition for running tests together.

items.prompt: Two tests both bind port 8080. What happens when they overlap?
choices: Both pass with double the speed
The runner picks a new port for both
One fails because the port is in use
items.explanation: A fixed port can be held by only one process.

items.prompt: How do you fix the hardcoded port?
choices: Pick a larger port number for all
Assign a port per worker or per test
Run those tests only on Fridays
items.explanation: A dynamic port gives each test its own.

items.prompt: Why did serial runs never show these bugs?
choices: Tests never overlapped in time
Serial runs skip hard tests
Serial runs use faster machines
items.explanation: One at a time means two tests never touch the same thing together.

items.prompt: Does parallelism create these bugs?
choices: Yes, it adds them to the code under test
Yes, but only in test files
No, it exposes ones already there
items.explanation: The isolation gap existed from the start.

items.prompt: A shared cache is never reset between tests. What goes wrong?
choices: The cache fills the disk at once
One test's leftovers change another's result
Tests run in a random order forever
items.explanation: Results then depend on what ran before.

items.prompt: How can a test protect shared database rows?
choices: Use a rollback or unique keys per test
Delete every row after each test
Share one single row id across all of the tests
items.explanation: Per-test data isolation stops cleanups from colliding.

items.prompt: What do all these hazards have in common?
choices: Each one needs a slow network
Each one is in the code under test
Something exists once and many tests use it
items.explanation: A single shared thing is the common shape.

items.prompt: A suite ran green serially for two years. After switching on 4-way parallelism, tests that never failed start failing at random. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Parallelism wrote new bugs into the application under test
Isolation was always missing and parallelism exposed it
The CI vendor changed something that broke these tests
The tests were fine and the failures are purely random
items.explanation: Serial order guaranteed overlap never happened, so a missing boundary stayed hidden.
items.reference:
Anything that exists once and is shared is a hazard
shared mutable state
hardcoded port or name
shared database rows
fixed temp file path
global cache never reset
Why: serial runs hide collisions because tests never overlap; parallel runs give them the chance.
items.learnMore:
Parallel-unsafe tests

Each hazard is a single shared thing that more than one test writes to or depends on. The fix pattern is always to give each test, or each worker, its own copy: fresh object, dynamic port, isolated rows, unique path, reset cache.

Common mistake

Saying parallelism caused the bug. It only exposed an isolation gap that was always there.
items.reflection: Think of two people who share a kitchen but have never cooked at the same time. What small thing would break the first evening they both do?

items.prompt: Two tests both write the file `report.tmp` in the working directory. Sometimes one reads the other's half-written content. What is the best fix?
choices: Make both tests sleep a little before they write
Run both tests twice and keep the passing result
Put a worker or test id in each test's file path
Make the file larger so it is written in one go
items.explanation: A unique path removes the shared thing. Sleeping and retrying only change how often the collision happens.

Make both tests use the same user id so the rows are identical
Remove the cleanup so rows pile up and nothing is ever deleted

items.prompt: In the trace, what does Test A's reset do to Test B?
choices: Sets B's counter back to zero mid-test
Makes B skip its remaining requests
Tells B how many requests it made
items.explanation: A's reset zeroes the counter B was relying on.

items.prompt: Where was the bug in the example?
choices: In the limiter's counting logic for requests
In the number of allowed requests
In how the tests shared one limiter
items.explanation: The limiter counted correctly; the setup was wrong.

items.prompt: What does the fix change?
choices: The limiter now blocks after four
Each test builds its own limiter
The tests now run only in order
items.explanation: One fresh limiter per test removes the sharing.

items.prompt: Why did the tests pass when run one at a time?
choices: They never overlapped in time
The limiter ignored the resets
The limit was set very high
items.explanation: Serial runs kept each test's counter use separate.

items.prompt: The limiter allows at most 3 requests. What should the 4th request get?
choices: Allowed
Queued for later
Blocked
items.explanation: Past the limit of three, requests are blocked.

items.prompt: After the fix, is the reset call still needed?
choices: Yes, to clear the old limiter
No, a fresh limiter starts at zero
Yes, to tell all of the other tests about it
items.explanation: A new limiter has nothing to clear.

items.prompt: Did the fix require editing the limiter module?
choices: No, only the test setup
Yes, the counting was wrong
Yes, it needed a lock
items.explanation: The module was never broken.

items.prompt: After the fix, in what order can the tests run?
choices: Only in the order A then B
Only on one single worker
Any order, in any number of shards
items.explanation: Nothing shared means order stops mattering.

items.prompt: In the trace, Test B's 4th request was allowed although the limit is 3. What actually happened?
choices: The limiter has a bug that lets one extra request through whenever two clients are active
Test A's reset zeroed the counter after B's second request, so B's 3rd and 4th counted as 1 and 2
Test B made only three requests, so the counter never reached the limit it checks
The limiter forgot B's first request because A and B use different reset calls
items.explanation: The counter went 2, reset to 0, then 1 (A), 2, 3. B's last request left it at 3 instead of being blocked.
items.reference:
One counter, two tests that reset it
B: reset, request 1, 2
A: reset (counter back to 0), request 1
B: request 3, 4 counted as 1, 2
B expected the 4th blocked, got allowed
Why: the bug is the tests' shared object, so the fix is one fresh object per test.
items.learnMore:
The fixture-per-test fix

The limiter counted honestly. The tests wrongly assumed the counter was theirs alone. Building the limiter inside each test removes the sharing, so any order, any number of shards gives the same answer.

Common mistake

Fixing the limiter, adding a lock to it, or retrying failures. None of them touches the tests' wrong assumption.
items.reflection: Where in your own work do two tasks quietly share one notebook or one tool? What would it look like to give each its own?

items.prompt: Which change removes the bug rather than hiding it?
choices: Retry any failed test up to three times
Run all tests one at a time on one worker
Create a fresh limiter inside each test
Add a lock around the limiter's counter
items.explanation: A fresh object per test removes the shared thing. Retries hide it, serial gives up speed, a lock protects an object that was never wrong.

Each limiter resets itself automatically a moment before every request
Each limiter copies the count from the previous test and continues it
Each limiter keeps its own private count that no other test can reach

items.prompt: A new test needs a large seeded database that is expensive to build. Which approach keeps isolation without rebuilding it for every test?
choices: Share the read-only seed, and give each test or worker its own writable copy or rolled-back transaction
Share one writable database across all tests and let each test clean up after itself at the very end of its run
Build the database once per day and run every test against that single copy
Disable the tests that write data so nothing ever needs to be isolated
items.explanation: Read-only sharing is safe. Writes need per-test or per-worker isolation.

items.prompt: What is quarantine?
choices: Moving a flaky test out of the blocking suite
Deleting a flaky test from the whole suite for good
Rerunning a flaky test until it passes
items.explanation: It is a tracked, non-blocking home for the test.

items.prompt: Does a quarantined test still run?
choices: No, it is switched off fully
Yes, and it still blocks merges
Yes, but it cannot fail a build
items.explanation: Its results stay visible without blocking.

items.prompt: Which three things go on a quarantine entry?
choices: Author, branch, build number
Owner, reason, revisit-by date
Priority, label, file size
items.explanation: Those three keep it tracked and time-boxed.

items.prompt: Why not just delete a flaky test?
choices: Its coverage would be gone untracked
Deleting it makes the whole suite run slower
Deleting breaks the CI pipeline
items.explanation: Whatever it checked would silently disappear.

items.prompt: Why not leave a flaky test blocking merges?
choices: It makes the suite finish faster
It makes the test pass more often
Reds get rerun and real ones get ignored
items.explanation: Noisy blocking trains the rerun habit.

items.prompt: What does the owner field give you?
choices: A list of everyone who edited it
A named person or team to act
A score for how flaky it is
items.explanation: A name turns 'someone should look' into a task.

items.prompt: What does the revisit-by date force?
choices: A decision: fix, extend or delete
A rerun of the whole suite
A move to the blocking suite
items.explanation: The date is the deadline for deciding.

items.prompt: Quarantine is best described as what?
choices: A permanent shelf
A way to skip testing
A time-boxed detour
items.explanation: It is meant to be temporary and tracked.

items.prompt: A team quarantined 15 tests with no owners or dates. Six months later it holds 40. What has the quarantine become?
choices: A healthy backlog that is shrinking as fixes land steadily
A second suite nobody trusts, now hidden instead of blocking
A faster replacement for the blocking suite it was taken from
A record that proves the quarantined tests are all useless
items.explanation: Without dates and owners the entries only accumulate, so the trust problem moved out of sight.
items.reference:
Quarantine: a tracked, time-boxed detour
flaky test leaves the blocking suite
still runs, cannot fail a build
owner + reason + revisit-by date
date reached: fix, or decide
Why: the date forces a decision; without it, the track fills with tests nobody trusts.
items.learnMore:
Quarantine is not deletion

A confirmed-flaky test is moved to a visible, non-blocking track so it stops causing false red builds. Its owner, reason and revisit-by date make sure it returns to the blocking suite or gets a deliberate decision.

Common mistake

Quarantining a test that fails every time because of a real regression. That is not flaky, it is a bug to fix.

items.prompt: Implement `isBlocking(testId, quarantinedIds)`: return `true` when `testId` is NOT in the `quarantinedIds` array.
items.explanation: A test blocks unless it is in the quarantined list.

items.prompt: Implement `hasAllFields(entry)`: return `true` only when `entry.owner`, `entry.reason` and `entry.revisitBy` are all non-empty strings.
items.explanation: All three fields must be truthy. Boolean() makes the result a real true or false.

items.prompt: Implement `isOverdue(revisitBy, today)`: both are ISO dates like `"2030-05-01"`. Return `true` when `revisitBy` is strictly before `today`.
items.explanation: ISO dates sort the same as plain strings, so a string comparison works. The same day is not overdue yet.

items.prompt: Implement `splitByQuarantine(ids, quarantinedIds)`: return `{ blocking, nonBlocking }`, each an array keeping the original order.
items.explanation: Two filters keep both lists in input order. The key order blocking, nonBlocking matches the expected shape.

items.prompt: Implement `shardFor(testIndex, shardCount)`: assign tests to shards round-robin, so test 0 goes to shard 0, test 1 to shard 1, and it wraps around.
items.explanation: The remainder after dividing by the shard count wraps the index around.

items.prompt: Implement `workPerShard(totalMinutes, shards)`: the evenly divided work each shard does, in minutes.
items.explanation: Even division of the total work.

items.prompt: Implement `missingFields(entry)`: return an array of the names among `owner`, `reason`, `revisitBy` that are missing or empty, in that order.
items.explanation: Filter the three required names down to the ones whose value is falsy, keeping their order.

items.prompt: Implement `countQuarantined(ids, quarantinedIds)`: how many of `ids` appear in `quarantinedIds`.
items.explanation: Keep the ids found in the quarantined list and count them.

items.prompt: Implement `overdueIds(entries, today)`. Each entry is `{ testId, revisitBy }` with an ISO date string. Return the `testId` of every entry whose `revisitBy` is strictly before `today`, in input order.
items.explanation: ISO dates compare correctly as strings. Filter to the entries strictly before today, then map to their ids. A date equal to today is not yet overdue.
items.reference:
A quarantine check is a small pure function
input: entries + today's date (passed in)
ISO dates compare as plain strings
output: ids the team must act on
Why: passing today in keeps the check testable, and the date comparison is what enforces the revisit-by rule.
items.learnMore:
Enforcing quarantine in code

The rules from L2 become checks over a list of entries: who is overdue, who is incomplete, which tests may block. Each is a filter over the list, and passing today's date in as an argument keeps it free of clocks and easy to test.

Common mistake

Using less-than-or-equal for overdue. A test due today still has today, so compare strictly.
items.reflection: Pick a rule you follow by habit, like reviewing a list every week. How could a small automatic check surface it when you forget?

items.prompt: Implement `routeTests(allIds, entries)`. `entries` is an array of `{ testId }` for quarantined tests. Return `{ blocking, nonBlocking }`: ids not in quarantine go to `blocking`, ids in quarantine to `nonBlocking`, each keeping input order.
items.explanation: Build a set of quarantined ids for fast lookup, then filter the full list both ways. Key order blocking, nonBlocking matches what the CI step expects.

items.prompt: Implement `incompleteEntries(entries)`. Each entry is `{ testId, owner, reason, revisitBy }`. Return the `testId` of every entry missing at least one of `owner`, `reason`, `revisitBy` (missing or empty string), in input order.

tests.expr: expect(incompleteEntries([{ testId: "a", owner: "x", reason: "y", revisitBy: "d" }, { testId: "b", owner: "x", reason: "", revisitBy: "d" }])).toEqual(["b"])

items.explanation: An entry is incomplete if any required field is falsy. Filter on that, then return the ids.
